doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Taking risks, simplicity and Vic Dickenson
summary: He tries anything on a swinging night, tells studio players to take chances, and has moved toward simplicity, as learned from Vic Dickenson.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you think about the quote safe notes in each chord as they go by, or is that more inherent by now?

I think by the time you get, if you’ve played as long as I have you know whether your chops are in good shape for instance on the given night, you know whether that band is swinging. If that band is swinging and your chops are in pretty good shape, I’ll try anything really, and I’m not worried about making a mistake. I’ve got enough confidence that what’s the worst that’s going to happen? I’m going to get fired? My reputation is going to go down the tubes because of one mistake or something? I’m not worried about it. I’d rather make it exciting. Even in the recording studio. I’ve seen some guys clutch up the minute — I know that they can really play hot. You put them on a record date in a recording studio, they will, everything is safe. And I’ll say afterwards “that isn’t you, man” I say don’t worry. Make a mistake. If worse comes to worse we’ll run it again. Well now you can edit in the note, edit out the note. But give me your best. I think that I probably, just strength wise, probably peaked maybe five or six years ago as far as high notes and things like that. And also I think I play a little bit more simply. Maybe this is

aging, maturity, call it what you want. I choose my notes but it’s a matter of choice. I don’t think I — I listened to myself when I thought I was great, playing very intense stuff, and I haven’t liked it as much as I thought I did when I was playing it. You know what I mean? So I’m a firm believer in simplicity. Vic Dickinson was the master of that and I played next to him for eight of the ten years we were at Condon’s. Just a master of simplicity. And he had marvelous technique, but he would just lay it out there, those beautiful melodies. So I love that.
